title: File Descriptors, Binary IO & Defensive Error Handling
summary: Master POSIX open/read/write/close versus standard C fopen/fread/fwrite, atomic file writes, binary struct serialization, and errno diagnostics.
learningObjectives: Differentiate unbuffered POSIX file descriptors (int fd) from buffered C streams (FILE*)
Serialize and deserialize binary structs with endianness considerations
Handle errors systematically using errno, strerror, and perror
prerequisiteConcepts: Completion of Module 2: Pointers & Dynamic Memory

sections.heading: 1. Buffered vs Unbuffered IO and Robust Error Handling
sections.content:
In C systems programming, two primary IO layers exist:
1. **Standard C Buffered IO (`<stdio.h>`):** `fopen`, `fread`, `fwrite`, `fclose`. Employs an internal user-space buffer to minimize kernel context switches. Ideal for general file processing.
2. **POSIX System Calls (`<fcntl.h>`, `<unistd.h>`):** `open`, `read`, `write`, `close`. Operates directly with raw kernel integer file descriptors (`int fd`). Ideal for socket programming, pipes, and non-blocking asynchronous IO.

**Defensive Error Handling with `errno`:**
C functions signal errors via sentinel return values (e.g., `NULL`, `-1`, or `EOF`). When an error occurs, the C runtime sets the thread-local global integer `errno`.
- `perror("message")`: Prints your custom message followed by the human-readable explanation of `errno`.
- `strerror(errno)`: Returns the string description of the error code for logging.

codeExamples.code:
C IO ARCHITECTURE:
User Application:      [ fread() / fwrite() ]       [ read() / write() ]
                               |                              |
Standard C Library:    [ stdio 4KB/8KB Buffer ]               |
                               | (Flushes on full / fflush)   |
Kernel Space:          [====== System Call (sys_read / sys_write) =====]
                               |
Hardware Device:       [ NVMe SSD / Hard Disk / Network Card ]
codeExamples.explanation: Standard C stdio buffers reduce expensive kernel system calls, while POSIX read/write interact directly with OS file descriptors.

keyPoints: Check return values of all file IO functions to detect disk full or permission errors.
Use binary mode ('rb', 'wb') when serializing structs to prevent newline conversions on Windows.
Always inspect errno immediately after a failed system call before another call overwrites it.
commonMistakes: Failing to close file handles with fclose/close, leading to file descriptor leaks.
Assuming fwrite writes all requested bytes in a single call without checking return counts.

sections.heading: 2. Atomic Binary Record Serialization Engine
sections.content: This program writes and verifies binary database records safely, checking write counts and handling errors via strerror.

codeExamples.explanation: Demonstrates packed binary struct serialization, file IO error verification with strerror, and checksum validation.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
Successfully wrote UserRecord 1001 to test_records.bin
Verified Record Integrity:
 - ID:       1001
 - Username: dev_scholar
 - Balance:  $2500.00
 - Checksum: 0x0003D45F (MATCH)

keyPoints: Always check fwrite/fread return counts to verify full records were read/written.
Use packed structs or explicit serialization serializers for disk-persistent binary formats.
commonMistakes: Assuming text-mode file IO works identically to binary mode on Windows.

sections.heading: 3. Systems Architecture Blueprint & Production Verification
sections.content:
Mastering File Descriptors, Binary IO & Defensive Error Handling requires continuous empirical verification. In production environments, verify that every memory allocation is accounted for, buffer boundaries are strictly honored, and execution logs provide deterministic diagnostics.

Key Operational Checks:
1. Validate inputs and boundary constraints before executing core business logic.
2. Structure error handling so failed operations release all acquired resources before returning.
3. Establish automated unit and regression tests that exercise edge conditions and stress boundaries.
keyPoints: Reliability in systems engineering is achieved by treating failure modes as first-class architectural concerns.
Document and verify performance invariants with repeatable benchmarks.
commonMistakes: Failing to profile and test under simulated peak load conditions.

exercises.title: Implement a File Copy Utility with Error Diagnostics
exercises.objective: Write a high-performance 4KB chunked file copy function in C.
exercises.description: Implement copy_file(const char *src, const char *dst) using a 4096-byte stack buffer and robust error checking.
instructions: Open src in 'rb' mode, dst in 'wb' mode.
Return false on any IO error and close open file pointers.
hints: Use while ((bytes_read = fread(buffer, 1, sizeof(buffer), src_fp)) > 0) to process chunks.
exercises.submissionRequirements: Complete all checklist items, test assumptions, and document verification rationale.
evaluationCriteria: Addresses the root architectural/technical challenge accurately
Follows defensive industry standards and edge-case validation
exercises.solutionExplanation: Chunked binary copying avoids loading massive files into RAM all at once.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Which C standard library function converts an errno integer into a human-readable string?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: strerror(errno) returns a pointer to the textual description of the corresponding error code.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Why must binary files be opened with 'rb' or 'wb' modes rather than plain 'r' or 'w'?

options.text: To prevent the C runtime from performing automatic newline translations (CRLF vs LF) on Windows platforms
Binary mode compresses the data automatically
Standard C does not support plain 'r' mode

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Text mode on Windows translates \n into \r\n on write and vice-versa on read, corrupting raw binary structs.

recap: File descriptors and C streams provide access to persistent storage. Packed structs, checksum validation, and errno diagnostics ensure data integrity.
